items.title: Allen Toussaint Interview, 1979-03-13
items.q: Actually, I had been playing with Earl King and Roland Cook, who was the bass player for Earl King.

ctx.x: But this has given you much, much greater control over the way your music comes out than for a lot of other musicians. And more control of really destiny.

Destiny. Destiny. Destiny. Well, maybe some things do. But I think musicians can, can be involved with the way that things come out. But it's such a responsibility to tell. I don't know if that's a curse or a blessing. To be responsible for spending someone's $150,000 on what you thought was right. Mm-hm. Actually, I had been playing with Earl King and Roland Cook, who was the bass player for Earl King. And there was a guy named Danny Kessler coming through town to pick artists and to search for talent. And he…

I don't think I've heard any tracks from that. Great. Great if you haven't. Something best left forgotten. Got some tape left on that. In 1965, if I'm not mistaken, we got together with Marshall Seahorn for Sansu Enterprises. And that's when you put out some great things about Lee Dorsey working in the coal mine. Holy Cow. Did those just come to you like driving in the car and things like that? Those are such, I think those kind of define the New Orleans fun song. Things that you always want to sing over and over…

items.title: Earl King Interview, 1980-04-10
items.q: Because, uh, the producers, Sue, uh, had a gear for music or something, they did pretty well. You know, like I did with Alton, you know.

ctx.x: Yeah. A lot of times, a lot of times, the bass was lost in a lot of recordings. Yeah. The fidelity of the mixing. So, uh, so we could say, maybe people look at all the instruments. We said the guitar was basically a rhythm instrument in New Orleans music. The bass and the drums, uh, carry the rhythm. And, uh, the horns, it seems the horns and the piano were basically the solo instruments. Yeah. And, uh, did, took care of most of the solos. Yeah. Um. Whereas in, in other parts of the country, Chicago, the guitar…

Uh, down here, there's another thing. And, and I think Sue was producing that, you know, it depends, you know. Because, uh, the producers, Sue, uh, had a gear for music or something, they did pretty well. You know, like I did with Alton, you know. Like they would be able to hear. And they would more guitar and Dave stuff with Imperial than any other label around here. You know, you know, because, many of the recordings, you will notice Imperial, you know. But, uh, other labels, because like I said, that phrase…
When record companies would come from Montana in the 1950s, and people would hear, tell me that story about how people would come to the studio to audition. What the audition process was?
